questions.stem: The points $P$, $Q$ and $R$ have coordinates $(-3, 7)$, $(9, 11)$ and $(12, 2)$ respectively.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Prove that angle $PQR = 90°$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
Way 1
M1: Attempts both gradients with an attempt at $\frac{\text{difference in }y}{\text{difference in }x}$ seen at least once, e.g. $\text{grad PQ} = \frac{11-7}{9-(-3)} = \frac{1}{3}$, $\text{grad QR} = \frac{11-2}{9-12} = -3$
A1: Achieves both correct gradients which may be left unsimplified
A1: e.g. $\frac{1}{3}\times -3 = -1$ so angle PQR $=90°$. Do not allow ambiguous statements for the explanation.
Way 2 (Pythagoras/cosine rule): M1A1: $PQ^2=160$, $QR^2=90$, $PR^2=250$ correct; A1: $PQ^2+QR^2=PR^2$ so angle PQR $=90°$
Way 3 (vectors): M1A1: $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\begin{pmatrix}12\\4\end{pmatrix}$, $\overrightarrow{QR}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-9\end{pmatrix}$; A1: $\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\overrightarrow{QR}=36-36=0$ so angle PQR $=90°$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- General Guidance for part (a): M1: Requires some correct work depending on the method. A1: Correct work for the chosen method. A1: Depends on both previous marks and requires an explanation and a conclusion. The conclusion must refer to angle PQR being 90° or equivalent e.g. "PQ and QR are perpendicular", "Q is 90", "Q is a right angle" etc. but condone e.g. "A = 90" or e.g. "$\theta$ = 90" if the solution is otherwise correct. This may occur in a preamble e.g. If grad PQ x Grad QR = −1 then PQR = 90, $\frac{11-7}{9--3}=\frac{1}{3}$, $\frac{11-2}{9-12}=-3$, $\frac{1}{3}\times-3=-1$ hence proven. Scores full marks.
- Way 1 A1: e.g. $\frac{1}{3}\times-3=-1\Rightarrow PQR=90°$ or e.g. $\frac{1}{3}$ is the negative reciprocal of – 3 so Q = 90. Do not allow ambiguous statements e.g. $\frac{1}{3}$ is the opposite inverse of – 3 for the explanation.
- NB: $\frac{11-7}{9--3}=\frac{1}{3}$, $\frac{11-2}{9-12}=-3$, $\frac{1}{3}\times-3=-1\Rightarrow PQR=90°$ would be a minimum for M1A1A1
- Way 2 M1: Attempts all three lengths with an attempt at "the difference between the coordinates" and "squaring" seen at least twice. Note that the "differences" may be implied by their answers or their lengths. A1: All three lengths or lengths$^2$ correct as single exact terms or as decimals – allow one d.p. Lengths are $\sqrt{160},\sqrt{90},\sqrt{250}$ or $4\sqrt{10},3\sqrt{10},5\sqrt{10}$ or e.g. 12.6, 9.5 (or 9.4 truncated), 15.8
- Way 2 A1: via Pythagoras or cosine rule e.g. $PQ^2+QR^2=PR^2$ so PQR = 90° or e.g. $\cos\theta=\frac{160+90-250}{2\sqrt{160}\sqrt{90}}=0\Rightarrow\theta=90°$. If via the cosine rule, all values must be in the correct positions with correct signs. "160, 90, 250 is a Pythagorean triple so PQR = 90°" is acceptable for the final mark. Values must appear as exact for this mark. E.g. $\cos\theta=\frac{12.6^2+9.5^2-15.8^2}{2\times12.6\times9.5}=0\Rightarrow\theta=90°$ scores M1A1A0
- Way 3 M1: Attempts $\pm\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and $\pm\overrightarrow{QR}$ with an attempt at "the difference between the coordinates" seen at least twice. A1: Correct vectors for $\pm\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and $\pm\overrightarrow{QR}$

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Given that the point $S$ is such that $PQRS$ forms a rectangle,
(b) find the coordinates of $S$.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Any suitable method of finding at least $x$ or $y$ for $S$. It can be implied by one correct coordinate which may be seen on a diagram. e.g. via vectors $(-3,7)+(3,-9)=(0,-2)$ or $(12,2)-(12,4)=(0,-2)$
A1: Correct coordinates $(0,-2)$ which may be written separately e.g. $x=0, y=-2$ or as $\begin{pmatrix}0\\-2\end{pmatrix}$
Alt 1: M1: Attempts the equation of line PS, the equation of line RS and solves simultaneously to find $x$ or $y$; A1: $(0,-2)$
Alt 2: M1: Attempts the midpoint of PR and uses Q to find S for at least one of $x$ or $y$; A1: $(0,-2)$

parts.text:

(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Attempts to write as a sum of two terms with one processed index correct. Award for $Px^3+Qx^k$ or $Px^k+Qx^{-2}$ or $Px^k+\frac{Q}{x^2}$ where $k$ could be $0$.

has no real roots, find the range of possible values for $k$.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:

questions.stem:
In this question you must show all stages of your working.
Solutions relying on calculator technology are not acceptable.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) By substituting $p = 3^x$, show that the equation
$3 \times 9^x + 3^{x+2} = 1 + 3^{x-1}$
can be rewritten in the form
$9p^2+26p-3=0$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: Uses an index law and states or implies any of $9^x=p^2$, $3^{x+2}=9p$ or $3^{x-1}=\frac{p}{3}$ or equivalent forms.
M1: Look for $3\times 9^x+3^{x+2}=1+3^{x-1} \Rightarrow 3p^2\pm kp = 1\pm\frac{p}{3}$ oe obtained from correct work, with $k=6$ or $9$. So if e.g. $3p^2$ is obtained from $3\times 9^x=3\times 3^2\times 3^x=3p^2$ or $3\times 9^x=3\times 3\times 3^x=3p^2$ then score M0.
A1*: Proceeds to the given answer of $9p^2+26p-3=0$ with no errors or omissions. An intermediate line of $3p^2+9p=1+\frac{p}{3}$ o.e. must be seen.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- (a) Mark (a) and (b) together.
- B1: ... e.g. $9^x=p\times p$, $3^{x+2}=3^2\times p$, $3^{x-1}=p\times3^{-1}$. If awarding for the first term, then it must be from correct work so $3\times9^x=3\times3^x\times3^x=3p^2$ is fine but $3\times9^x=3\times3^2\times3^x=3p^2$ or $3\times9^x=3\times3\times3^x=3p^2$ is not, but do check the other terms.
- Note that the following is common in part (a) and scores no marks: $3\times9^x+3^{x+2}=1+3^{x-1}\Rightarrow3\times3p+p^2=1+p^{-1}$

parts.text:
(b) Hence solve
$3 \times 9^x + 3^{x+2} = 1 + 3^{x-1}$
(3)

M1: Valid non-calculator attempt at solving $9p^2+26p-3=0$. It must be clear they are solving the given quadratic not their incorrect one. Answers just written down score M0. e.g. $(9p-1)(p+3)=0$
A1 (M1 in EPEN): For $3^x=\frac{1}{9}$ seen. It must be clear that it is a value for $3^x$ and not a value for $p$ or $x$. May be implied by e.g. $p=\frac{1}{9}\Rightarrow x=-2$. You can ignore e.g. $3^x=-3$ for this mark.

ddM1: Attempts to solve cubic of the form $ax^3+bx^2=0$ by taking out a factor of $x^2$ or e.g. by division by $x^2$ leading to a value for $x$. Depends on both previous M marks. May be implied by e.g. $ax^3+bx^2=0 \Rightarrow x=-\frac{b}{a}$
A1: $x=-\frac{67}{6}$ and no other solutions apart from $x=0$ which can be ignored. Ignore any attempts to find $y$.
Note: just an incorrect $x$ coefficient in the expansion in (b) will result in $x=-\frac{67}{6}$ in (c) if the subsequent work is correct — allow full recovery in (c). Similarly if the expansion in (b) is e.g. divided by 6, allow full recovery.

questions.stem:
A curve $C$ has equation $y=\mathrm{f}(x)$, $\qquad x>0$
Given that
• $\mathrm{f}''(x)=4x+\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$
• the point $P$ has $x$ coordinate 4 and lies on $C$
• the tangent to $C$ at $P$ has equation $y=3x+4$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) find an equation of the normal to $C$ at $P$
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: States or implies that the gradient of the normal is $-\frac{1}{3}$
A1: Correct equation of normal e.g. $y-16=-\frac{1}{3}(x-4)$. Requires a full correct equation. Apply isw once a correct equation is seen. But not $\frac{y-16}{x-4}=-\frac{1}{3}$.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- A1: Finds the equation of the normal $y-16=-\frac{1}{3}(x-4)$ o.e. e.g. $y=-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{52}{3}$, $3y+x-52=0$

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) find $\mathrm{f}(x)$, writing your answer in simplest form.
(6)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Attempts to integrate $\mathrm{f}''(x)$ once with one index correct. E.g. $4x\to\ldots x^2$ or $\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\to\ldots x^{\frac{1}{2}}$
dM1: Applies $\mathrm{f}'(4)=3$ and solves to find a constant of integration. Depends on first M1.
A1: $(\mathrm{f}'(x)=)2x^2+2x^{\frac{1}{2}}-33$ or obtains $(\mathrm{f}'(x)=)2x^2+2x^{\frac{1}{2}}+c$ with $c$ correctly calculated as $-33$
dM1: Dependent upon first M1 only. For an attempt to integrate $\mathrm{f}''(x)$ twice and achieve a form $(\mathrm{f}(x)=)ax^3+bx^{\frac{3}{2}}+\ldots$ where $\ldots$ could be $0$.
ddM1: Dependent upon all previous M's. It is for using $\mathrm{f}(4)=16$ (may be implied) to find the constant of integration.
A1: $(\mathrm{f}(x)=)\frac{2}{3}x^3+\frac{4}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}}-33x+\frac{284}{3}$ or exact equivalent. Apply isw once a correct expression is seen. The "$\mathrm{f}(x)=$" is not required.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- (b) Award marks if work in (b) is seen in (a).
- Ignore labelling of the function e.g. they may call it f (x)
- The "f(x) =" is not required and ignore any label they may have given it. Also allow $(f(x)=)\frac{2}{3}x^3+\frac{4}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}}-33x+c$ with c correctly calculated as $\frac{284}{3}$.
